content: The most frequently reported challenge in providing care to adolescents living with HIV is non-adherence to treatment and the development of treatment resistance, as noted by 40% of survey respondents. This issue was highlighted as the most significant barrier to effective care. The second most common challenge, cited by 30% of respondents, is the non-disclosure of HIV status. This includes both the failure to disclose the diagnosis to the adolescent (43% of those citing this challenge) and the adolescent’s reluctance to disclose their status to others (21%). The remaining 36% of respondents did not specify which category of non-disclosure they were referring to. Socio-economic barriers, such as poverty, transportation costs due to long distances to healthcare facilities, and food insecurity, were identified as challenges by 25% of respondents. Additionally, 24% of respondents highlighted inadequate resources and space limitations in healthcare facilities as significant obstacles. Other commonly cited challenges include stigma, myths surrounding HIV, reliance on traditional medicine, behavioral issues among adolescents, drug fatigue, denial of their condition, poor caregiver support or orphanhood, loss to follow-up, and staff shortages or lack of training. Less frequently mentioned challenges include the unavailability of appropriate drug formulations, stockouts of medications, lack of adolescent-friendly services or materials, difficulties addressing the sexual and reproductive health needs of adolescents, patient mobility and relocation, side effects of treatment, pill burden, challenges in boarding school environments, mental health issues, transition-related difficulties, opportunistic infections, delayed presentation for care, and substance abuse. A significant proportion of facilities (26%) reported not having an official working definition of adolescence. This issue is particularly pronounced in West and Central Africa, where 49% of facilities lack such a definition. Definitions of adolescence vary widely, with the reported age range for the onset of adolescence spanning from 8 to 21 years. While 57% of facilities define the start of adolescence at 10 years of age, only 13% define the start of adulthood at 20 years. In terms of record-keeping, 66% of facilities maintain records that allow for the identification of adolescents within the overall patient population. However, 18% of facilities do not distinguish between children, adolescents, and adults in their records. In 11% of facilities, adolescents are recorded as children, and in 4%, they are recorded as adults. West and Central African countries report the lowest rates of adolescent identification in facility records, at 53%. The most commonly recorded descriptor for adolescents living with HIV is pregnancy status (69%), followed by whether the adolescent was perinatally infected (37%). Other descriptors, such as key population status (e.g., young people who sell sex, inject drugs, or engage in same-sex relationships), are recorded in only 14–18% of facilities. Notably, 25% of facilities across all regions do not record any of these descriptors. Regarding treatment outcomes, only 20% of facilities disaggregate treatment outcomes by age. However, 75% of facilities track first-line treatment regimens, 72% track second-line regimens, and 17% track third-line regimens. Loss-to-follow-up rates are recorded in 77% of facilities, while treatment failure, mortality, and virological suppression rates are monitored in 69%, 63%, and 43% of facilities, respectively. East African facilities report better monitoring of treatment outcomes compared to their counterparts in West, Central, and Southern Africa, except for third-line treatment outcomes, which are best monitored in Southern Africa. Alarmingly, 42% of facilities in West and Central Africa do not monitor any treatment outcomes. The most common clinical presentations among adolescents living with HIV include delayed growth and puberty (89%), skin conditions (84%), and opportunistic infections (77%). Other presentations include chronic lung disease (48%), mental health issues (41%), neurocognitive impairment (21%), lipoatrophy (9%), and malnutrition (7%). When switching adolescents to second-line antiretroviral therapy (ART), the primary challenge reported by facilities is ongoing adherence difficulties (84%). Other challenges include defining treatment failure in the absence of viral load monitoring (48%), lack of second-line treatment options (27%), and lack of appropriate drug formulations (20%). Less common challenges include side effects (9%), pill burden (7%), poor caregiver support or orphanhood (5%), staff knowledge and skills (2%), and laboratory issues (2%). Efforts to improve treatment adherence among adolescents include offering specific services rather than relying solely on guidelines or protocols. Approximately 67% of facilities provide such services, with East African facilities being the most likely to offer them (84%), followed by Southern Africa (68%) and West and Central Africa (44%). Common adherence support activities include peer support groups, home visits, adherence counseling, and general counseling. Peer support activities, in particular, are considered highly effective, as they foster a sense of community and allow adolescents to share personal experiences and solutions to common problems. Adherence counseling is offered in 87% of facilities, with the highest rates in East Africa (97%), followed by Southern Africa (90%) and West and Central Africa (69%). Counseling sessions often focus on the importance of adherence to ART, the implications of non-adherence (e.g., resistance), and the risks of opportunistic infections and mortality. Less frequently, counseling addresses topics such as positive living, sexual and reproductive health, emotional well-being, disclosure support, and strategies for accessing social support.
